title: Once in a thousand years
hook: how people would marvel if the stars appeared only one night in a thousand years (Nature 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emerson's Nature: if a man would be alone, let him look at the stars. Your line was under the stars. Did you get a minute of sky? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

A grocery store parking lot after dark. Someone is loading bags into a trunk, checking the receipt, finding the keys. Above them, the whole sky is doing what it does every clear night. They don't look up. Nobody would blame them. It's always there. But that's exactly the trouble Emerson puts his finger on, a few lines after he sends us out under the stars. He asks what would happen if the sky weren't always there. Today, once in a thousand years.
screen: `A PARKING LOT AFTER DARK.` → `NOBODY LOOKS UP.` → `IT'S ALWAYS THERE.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. "If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and adore; and preserve for many generations the remembrance of the city of God which had been shown!" Crowds on every roof. Stories handed down to grandchildren. A night people would date their lives by. Second, the turn. "But every night come out these envoys of beauty, and light the universe with their admonishing smile." Envoys: messengers sent with something to deliver. They come every night, and because they come every night, we stop answering the door. Third, that odd word, admonishing. An admonishing smile is a smile that also corrects you, kindly. The stars aren't scolding. But their steady return is a quiet reminder of what we've stopped noticing. Emerson goes on to say the stars stir a kind of reverence because they're always present and yet out of reach. Fourth, what this means between one breakfast and the next. The trouble isn't that wonder is rare. It's that the things worth wonder are common, and so they become furniture. A face you see every morning. The fact that water comes out of a tap. Rain on a roof. Emerson isn't asking for new sights. He's asking for new eyes on the old ones. He calls the stars envoys of beauty, and the envoys keep coming whether anyone answers. The practice is simply to answer once.
screen: `ONE NIGHT IN A THOUSAND YEARS.` · `BUT EVERY NIGHT THEY COME.` · `AN ADMONISHING SMILE.` · `COMMON THINGS BECOME FURNITURE.` · then, large: `ENVOYS OF BEAUTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look as if for the first time. Choose one ordinary thing within sight: your hand, a cup, a window, a plant, the ceiling. Now look at it as though it appears only once in a thousand years, and this is the night. Notice its color, its edges, how the light sits on it. When your mind says I know what that is, look again anyway. Let it be strange for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Once in a thousand years. Emerson's thought that if the stars came out that rarely, people would believe and adore, and yet they come out every night. Today's word.
screen: `ONCE IN A THOUSAND YEARS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: once in a thousand years. Today, pick one face or one thing you see every day, and give it one look as if it might never come around again. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of Emerson sometimes use this passage from Nature as a prompt for looking at familiar things, a night sky, a face, a street, as if seeing them for the first time.
